messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: One Global detection function,
parts:
Since your goal is to get area-time specific estimates, create 6 strata
with one for each area and time. Use all of the data for a species or
group of species to estimate detection probability and then get
stratum-specific estimates of abundance by species. Because they use
the same detection function across strata they will have covariances so
you'll have to deal with that but only if you want to combine them. You
do have a couple of options here.
1) You can use CDS and use data filter to get the species (or species
group), fit the detection function (globally) and get stratum specific
abundance estimates.
That will work fine except for the species groups because you won't be
able to get density of each species within the group.
2) You can use MCDS and do the same as above but also consider area/time
or both as covariates to see if it is safe to assume that detection for
a species doesn't vary across time/area. They same can be done with CDS
but is rather kludgy to do because you have to split out each data set
(species-area-time), fit the models, sum AICs and compare to AIC without
area-time. But with CDS you can't fit additive models of area and time
and you can in MCDS. Still the downside is that you still can't compute
species-specific estimates of abundance within a group of species pooled
to estimate the detection function.
3) You can use MRDS which was designed for double-observer surveys but
has a single-observer mode which is equivalent to MCDS with 2 big
differences. First, it will not use adjustment functions like with
CDS/MCDS. But, it will let you fit a common detection function to a
group of species and then get species-specific estimates within that
group by running a separate analysis that filters for each species and
then applies the common detection function. Additionally, it will output
the variance-covariance matrix of stratum specific estimates so you can
sum the estimates and construct the correct variance which is the sum of
the variances and covariances for the set being summed.

regards --jeff

Adrian Gall wrote:
> > Dear List,
> >
> > I am struggling with a large and sprawling dataset and could use some
> > guidance on analysis. The data are line-transect visual detections stratified by
> > study area (n=2) and collected during three time periods. I would like to
> > generate 6 density estimates for each of the 45 species in the dataset, one
> > estimate for each study-area-time-period. So far, I have estimated detection
> > functions for the 10 species that have obs > 60. I have assigned each of the
> > remaining 35 rare species (obs n = 2-20) to a "detection group" based on their
> > similarities to more abundant species (following Alldredge et al 2007). My plan
> > is to use the Multiplier to estimate densities for the rare species based on the
> > abundant species in their detection group. Now I am stalled out trying to
> > decide how to apply the global detection function to estimates for each study-
> > area-time-period. The data are currently structured with Stratum = Study
> > Area, Sample = Time period, and Subsample = transect.
> >
> > Options I am considering:
> > 1. Separate Projects for each time period, use Study area to stratify.
> > 2. Creating a single Stratum field that designates 6 strata, one for each study-
> > area-time-period.
> >
> > The biggest problem is that one of the study areas has far fewer detections
> > than the other one, so I need all the observations from both study areas to
> > generate a pooled detection function. There is little reason to suspect a
> > difference in detection rate between the study areas. Any advice on how to
> > tackle this beast would be much appreciated.
> >
> > Thanks!
> > Adrian

messages.author: 2a118b9e34b31895
messages.subject: Re: One Global detection function,
parts:
Hi Adrian, List,

I have another idea:

1. assign separate strata for each combination of area-time-species=20
2. filter for a given species group=20
3. fit a global detection function=20
4. estimate stratum-specific density estimates

The only difference from Jeff's option #2 is that strata include
species, in addition to area and time. Jeff reminded me to make sure you
correctly assign effort by area-time, regardless of species.

I'm planning on doing this same thing with my dataset, which sounds
similar to yours. Feel free to contact me off list if you'd like to get
more into the gritty details.

Best,
Chris

Chris Merkord
University of Missouri
Columbia, MO, USA
clme...@mizzou.edu
